title: Sentences without a doer
goal: Face the most distinctive feature of Icelandic: when the topic is feelings, "I" stops being the doer and becomes the target — and the word's form changes with it.
bekal: use *mér finnst*, *mér líður*, *mér er kalt*, and *mér líkar*
tell the expressions that take *mér* from those that take *mig*
express opinions, feelings, and needs naturally

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hvernig líður þér?
dialogs.intro: Early November. The days are getting shorter, and Búdí is feeling the Icelandic winter for the first time.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Mér líður vel, takk. En mér er kalt.
lines.id: I'm fine, thanks. But I'm cold.
lines.literal: to-me feels well, thanks. but to-me is cold.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Auðvitað — það er vindur. Mér er alltaf kalt í nóvember.
lines.id: Of course — it's the wind. I'm always cold in November.
lines.literal: of-course — it is wind. to-me is always cold in November.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.id: I find the Icelandic winter hard.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Mér finnst hann fallegur. En mér leiðist myrkrið.
lines.id: I think it's beautiful. But I'm tired of the darkness.
lines.literal: to-me seems it beautiful. but to-me bores darkness-the.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.id: When does it get light again?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Í mars. Þá langar okkur öll út.
lines.id: In March. Then we all want to get outside.
lines.literal: in March. then longs us all out.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Mér líkar vel við Ísland, en mig vantar sól.
lines.id: I like Iceland, but I'm missing the sun.
lines.literal: to-me likes well with Iceland, but me lacks sun.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Þig vantar bara D-vítamín, eins og okkur hin.
lines.id: You're just short of vitamin D, like all of us.
lines.literal: you(object) lacks only D-vitamin, one and us others.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Bíddu — af hverju segirðu „mér" og „mig", ekki „ég"?
lines.id: Wait — why do you say "mér" and "mig", not "ég"?
lines.literal: wait — of what say-you to-me and me, not I?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Af því að tilfinningin gerir eitthvað við þig. Þú ert ekki gerandinn.
lines.id: Because the feeling does something to you. You're not the doer.
lines.literal: of that that feeling-the does something at you. you are not doer-the.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Þá er íslenskan heiðarleg. Mér finnst það gott.
lines.id: Then Icelandic is honest. I like that.
lines.literal: then is Icelandic-the honest. to-me seems that good.

notes: **This is the big idea of the unit: feelings HAPPEN to you, you don't do them.** *Mér er kalt* is literally "to-me is cold". Not *ég er kaldur* — that sentence exists, but it means "I am a cold-hearted person".

**Two groups, with different cases.** Most take **þágufall** (*mér finnst*, *mér líður*, *mér líkar*, *mér leiðist*, *mér er kalt*); a small group takes **þolfall** (*mig langar*, *mig vantar*, *mig minnir*). No rule explains the split; learn each one with its word.

**And English still has traces of the same idea.** "It seems to me", "it occurs to me", the old "methinks" (= it seems to me) — the person is the one things happen to, not the doer. *Mér finnst* is "it seems to me", word for word. Only the forms are new, not the way of thinking.

**Mér finnst is followed by an adjective describing the THING**, not the person: *Mér finnst hann falleg**ur*** (*vetur* kk), *mér finnst hún falleg* (kvk), *mér finnst það gott* (hk). So the noun genders from unit 3 keep working.
**Mér líkar vel við + þolfall** — note the *við* in the middle. *Mér líkar vel við hana* = I like her. Without *við*, the sentence is incomplete.

**Myrkrið is a real issue in Iceland, not small talk.** In Reykjavík the sun rises at 11:20 and sets at 15:30 at the end of December — four hours of light. Vitamin D is sold in every supermarket and taken by almost everyone. In June, by contrast, the sun hardly sets at all.

grammars.title: Expressions with þágufall (mér)
body: The biggest group. They're all about what is **felt**, and they all put the person in the form *mér*, *þér*, *honum*, *henni*, *okkur*, *ykkur*, *þeim*.
after: ⚠️ *Ég er kaldur* and *mér er kalt* are very different sentences. The first describes a character (cold, unfeeling); the second says what someone feels. Choosing wrong here leads to misunderstandings that are funny, but real.
*Mér þykir vænt um þig* is the most common way Icelanders express affection — to family, friends, and partners. *Ég elska þig* exists, but it feels much bigger and is used far less.

grammars.title: Expressions with þolfall (mig)
body: A small group, but full of words you'll use every day.
after: *Langa* is followed by **í** when what you want is a thing (*mig langar í kaffi*), and by **að** when it's an action (*mig langar að sofa*).
Asking someone else: the person's form changes, the verb stays. *Langar **þig** í kaffi?* *Vantar **þig** hjálp?* Notice there's no *þú* in those sentences at all.

blocks.title: Why some take ég and some take mér
items: **Tired, hungry, thirsty** take *ég* and a normal adjective — because they describe **the state of your body**, and the adjective follows your gender: *þreyttur* (male), *þreytt* (female).
**Cold, hot, pain, boredom** take *mér* — because the topic isn't you but **what's happening to you**.
The line between the two doesn't always make sense, and even native speakers can't explain it. Learn the list; it isn't long.

sections.title: Light and dark through the year

blocks.text: Day length in Iceland swings more wildly than most places you've probably lived. This isn't just a cultural note: it shapes everyday conversation all year round.

*Skammdegi* is literally "short days", and Icelanders use it as a noun: *skammdegið er erfitt* — the dark season is hard. If you want one sentence that instantly makes you sound like a local in January, that's the one.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with *mér* or *mig*.

items: I'm cold: ____ (Ég er kaldur, Mér er kalt).
I'm tired: ____ (Mér er þreytt, Ég er þreyttur).
I think this is beautiful: ____ (Ég finn þetta fallegt, Mér finnst þetta fallegt).
I like her: ____ (Ég líka hana, Mér líkar vel við hana).
I'm hungry: ____ (Mig er svangur, Ég er svangur).

answers: Mér — Mig — Mér — Mig — Mér — Mér
Finnst þér þetta gott? — Langar þig í kaffi? — Er þér kalt? — Vantar þig hjálp? — Líður þér vel?
Mér er kalt — Ég er þreyttur — Mér finnst þetta fallegt — Mér líkar vel við hana — Ég er svangur
Hvernig líður þér í dag? — Mér líður vel, takk. — Mér er kalt. — Mér finnst veturinn erfiður. — Mig langar í kaffi. — Mig vantar hjálp.
